title: Collecting pollen with a pollen trap
subtitle: Setting up and running a hive entrance trap for fresh bee pollen.
excerpt: A pollen trap fits over the hive entrance and strips a proportion of the pollen loads from incoming foragers as they squeeze through a grid. The beekeeper collects the pellets from a drawer below. The technique is straightforward but the trap must be used intermittently: removing all pollen from every forager for more than a week damages the colony's nutrition.
sourceNotes: BBKA advisory resources on hive products (2022). NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on hive products. Erik Osterlund, Elgon bees and pollen trapping (2019). Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pollen grains collected by a foraging bee, mixed with nectar and packed into the corbiculae (pollen baskets) on the bee's hind legs. Each pellet can weigh 10 to 30 mg.
The pollen baskets on the hind legs of a foraging bee: concave smooth-sided areas fringed with stiff hairs that hold a compacted pollen pellet.

content.text: A pollen trap fits across the hive entrance and strips
pollen pellets
from foragers'
corbiculae

as they squeeze through a wire or plastic grid on the way in. The knocked-off pellets fall into a removable tray below for daily collection. Fresh pollen keeps for a day or two at room temperature, several weeks in the fridge, and a year in the freezer.
Types of trap

Bottom-board traps replace the hive floor; entrance traps clip to the front of the existing floor. Both work by making bees squeeze through a grid with holes sized to catch pollen pellets without injuring the bees. Entrance traps are simpler to fit and remove.
When to use it

Spring is the most productive period: foragers bring in willow, hazel, blackthorn, and fruit-tree pollen in large quantities from late February through May. The pellets are colourful (willow is bright yellow, hawthorn is cream, borage is grey-blue) and nutritionally varied.
Fitting the trap
Fit the trap to the hive entrance in the morning when bees are active and foraging is underway. This lets you watch that bees can get through the grid without difficulty before leaving them all day.

Check that drones can exit. Most traps have a side slot or a bypass opening: drones are too large for the pollen grid and will die inside the hive if there is no drone exit. The trap packaging usually states whether a drone exit is needed for your hive type.
Empty the collection drawer each morning. Pollen left in the drawer for more than two days in warm weather begins to ferment.
How long to run the trap

Do not run the trap continuously for more than three to four days on any one colony. A trap in continuous use removes most of the incoming pollen from the colony: brood rearing slows, young bee development suffers, and colony health declines if pollen is stripped for a week or more. The standard practice is to run the trap for two to three days, then remove it for a week before running again. This keeps the colony healthy and still yields a useful amount of pollen.
Drying and storing collected pollen
Spread fresh pellets in a single layer on a fine mesh tray. Dry at room temperature out of direct sunlight for 24 hours, or at no more than 40 degrees in a food dehydrator for four to six hours.
Store dried pollen in an airtight jar. It keeps for up to three months at room temperature or a year in the freezer.
Do not mix batches from different days: older pellets mixed with fresh ones bring moisture into the stored jar.

Pollen harvested for human consumption requires food hygiene registration if sold commercially in the UK. For personal use in the kitchen, standard food-grade hygiene applies. Some people are allergic to bee-collected pollen; anyone with hay fever or pollen allergies should take advice before trying it.

attrs.cue: Bees cannot get through the trap grid
attrs.cause: Grid size may be wrong for your bee strain, or foragers are loaded with extra-large pellets
attrs.fix: Check the trap specification against your hive type. A grid with 4.7 mm holes suits most UK honeybees. Remove the trap and check for bee mortality: if bees are dying at the entrance, the grid is too small.

attrs.cue: Very little pollen collecting in the tray
attrs.cause: Few foragers returning with loads, or the grid is missing pellets
attrs.fix: Check the hive entrance from below: are pellets visible dropping through? If foragers are coming in without pollen loads, there may be no good pollen source in flight range at this time of year.
